decks.title: Three-Dimensional Geometry: Lines — Part 1: Direction, angles and equations
goals: Find the direction cosines and direction ratios of a line through two points
Write the equations of the coordinate axes and coordinate planes
Find the angle between two lines and test whether they are perpendicular or parallel
Write the vector and Cartesian equations of a line and convert between them

slides.heading: Three-Dimensional Geometry: Lines, Part 1
slides.body_md: Straight lines in space, from a direction to an equation.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: direction cosines and ratios, equations of the axes and coordinate planes, the angle between two lines, and the vector and Cartesian equations of a line.
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance.

slides.narration: Welcome to lines in three dimensions. Drone paths, cables, tunnels and laser beams are all straight lines in space. In this part we describe the direction of a line with direction cosines and ratios, write the equations of the axes, find the angle between two lines, and finally write the equation of a line in vector and Cartesian form.

slides.heading: What you will learn

rows: find direction cosines and ratios of a line through two points
write the equations of the axes and coordinate planes
find the angle between two lines; test perpendicular and parallel
write a line in vector and Cartesian form

visual.alt: Table of the four goals of Part 1: direction cosines and ratios, equations of axes and coordinate planes, angles between lines, and the two forms of the equation of a line.
visual.caption: Four skills for Part 1.

slides.narration: Here are the four skills for this part. Each one builds on the one before, so work through them in order. By the end you will be able to take two points in space and write the full equation of the line through them.

slides.heading: Direction cosines
slides.body_md: If a line makes angles $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ with the axes, $l = \cos\alpha$, $m = \cos\beta$, $n = \cos\gamma$ and $l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$.

visual.alt: A three dimensional sketch with x, y and z axes drawn from the origin O, and a segment from O to a point P in space. The segment makes angles alpha, beta and gamma with the three axes.
visual.caption: $OP$ makes angles $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ with the axes: $l = \cos\alpha$, $m = \cos\beta$, $n = \cos\gamma$ (sketch, not to scale).

slides.narration: Draw the line through the origin and measure the angles it makes with the x, y and z axes. The cosines of these three angles are the direction cosines, usually called l, m and n. Because they are the components of a unit vector, the sum of their squares is always one. That fact is the quickest test of whether three numbers can be direction cosines.

slides.heading: Direction ratios
slides.body_md: Any three numbers proportional to $l, m, n$ are direction ratios. Divide by $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}$ to get the cosines.

visual.alt: Table: direction ratios 6, minus 3, 2 have length 7 and direction cosines 6 over 7, minus 3 over 7, 2 over 7; doubling the ratios gives length 14 and the same cosines; reversing every sign reverses the cosines.
visual.caption: Many sets of ratios describe one line; dividing by the length gives the cosines.

slides.narration: Direction cosines are often fractions, so we also use direction ratios, which are any three numbers proportional to them. A line has many sets of ratios but only two sets of cosines, one for each sense along the line. To go from ratios to cosines, divide each ratio by the square root of the sum of their squares, as the table shows.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: cosines of a line through two points
slides.body_md: Find the direction cosines of the line from $A(3, -2, 1)$ to $B(5, 4, -2)$.

visual.alt: A sketch of the axes with a segment from A, at 3, minus 2, 1, to B, at 5, 4, minus 2. The differences of the coordinates give the direction ratios of the line.
visual.caption: $\vec{AB} = 2\hat{i} + 6\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$, $AB = 7$ (sketch, not to scale).

slides.narration: Subtract the coordinates of A from those of B to get the direction ratios two, six and minus three. The length is the square root of four plus thirty six plus nine, which is seven. Divide each ratio by seven to get the direction cosines. A quick check: the squares add up to forty nine over forty nine, which is one.

slides.heading: Worked example 1 in a table
slides.body_md: Subtract, measure, divide, check.

visual.alt: Worked example 1 table: the ratios are 2, 6 and minus 3; the length is 7; the direction cosines are 2 over 7, 6 over 7 and minus 3 over 7; their squares add up to 1.
visual.caption: Subtract, measure, divide, check.

slides.narration: Here is the same working laid out as four steps. Writing the ratios and the length before the cosines earns the method marks, even if an arithmetic slip creeps in later.

slides.heading: Quick check: a beam at equal angles
slides.body_md: Find the direction cosines of a beam equally inclined to the three axes.

visual.alt: Table: direction ratios 6, minus 3, 2 have length 7 and direction cosines 6 over 7, minus 3 over 7, 2 over 7; doubling the ratios gives length 14 and the same cosines; reversing every sign reverses the cosines.
visual.caption: Many sets of ratios describe one line; dividing by the length gives the cosines.

slides.narration: If all three angles are equal, all three cosines are equal. Use the fact that their squares add up to one.

slides.heading: Equations of the axes and coordinate planes
slides.body_md: An axis is the meeting of two coordinate planes, so it needs two equations.

visual.alt: Table: the x axis is y equals 0 and z equals 0 with direction cosines 1, 0, 0; the y axis is x equals 0 and z equals 0; the z axis is x equals 0 and y equals 0; the coordinate planes are z equals 0, x equals 0 and y equals 0.
visual.caption: An axis needs two equations; a coordinate plane needs one.

slides.narration: On the x axis, both y and z are zero, so the x axis is described by two equations, y equals zero and z equals zero. Similarly for the other axes. A coordinate plane needs only one equation: the plane containing the x and y axes is z equals zero. Keep this difference clear, because a single equation in space is never a line.

slides.heading: A point on the vertical axis
slides.body_md: Every point of the $z$-axis has the form $(0, 0, t)$.

visual.alt: A sketch of the three coordinate axes from the origin. A point on the z axis is labelled 0, 0, t, showing that x and y are both zero on that axis.
visual.caption: On the $z$-axis, $x = 0$ and $y = 0$ (sketch, not to scale).

slides.narration: Picture a flagpole standing along the z axis. Whatever its height, a point on it has x equal to zero and y equal to zero. That is exactly why the z axis is written as x equals zero, y equals zero.

slides.heading: Angle between two lines
slides.body_md: Use direction ratios of the two lines; the modulus gives the acute angle.

headers: Condition on ratios $a_1, b_1, c_1$ and $a_2, b_2, c_2$

visual.alt: Table: the cosine of the angle between two lines is the absolute value of the sum of products of their direction ratios divided by the product of their lengths; a zero sum of products means perpendicular; proportional ratios mean parallel.
visual.caption: Only the directions matter for angles.

slides.narration: The angle between two lines depends only on their directions. Multiply corresponding direction ratios and add; divide by the product of the two lengths; take the modulus to get the acute angle. If the sum of products is zero, the lines are perpendicular. If the ratios are proportional, the lines are parallel.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the angle between two struts
slides.body_md: Find the angle between lines with direction ratios $1, 2, 2$ and $4, 0, 3$.

visual.alt: Worked example 2 table: for ratios 1, 2, 2 and 4, 0, 3 the sum of products is 10, the lengths are 3 and 5, and the cosine of the angle is two thirds.
visual.caption: $\theta = \cos^{-1}\dfrac23$.

slides.narration: Multiply the ratios pair by pair: one times four, two times zero and two times three give ten. The lengths are three and five. So the cosine of the angle is ten over fifteen, which is two thirds, and the angle is the inverse cosine of two thirds.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: perpendicular or parallel
slides.body_md: Find $k$ so that $2, -1, k$ is perpendicular to $3, 2, -1$; then test $2, -1, 3$ against $-4, 2, -6$.
bullets: **Parallel —** every ratio is $-2$ times the first

visual.alt: Worked example 3 table: ratios 2, minus 1, k and 3, 2, minus 1 are perpendicular when 6 minus 2 minus k equals 0, that is k equals 4; ratios 2, minus 1, 3 and minus 4, 2, minus 6 are parallel because each pair has ratio minus 2.
visual.caption: Zero sum of products, or equal ratios.

slides.narration: For perpendicular lines, the sum of products must be zero: six minus two minus k equals zero, so k is four. For the second pair, each ratio of the second line is minus two times the corresponding ratio of the first, so those lines are parallel.

slides.heading: Quick check: two roof struts
slides.body_md: Find the acute angle between the struts.

headers: Condition on ratios $a_1, b_1, c_1$ and $a_2, b_2, c_2$

visual.alt: Table: the cosine of the angle between two lines is the absolute value of the sum of products of their direction ratios divided by the product of their lengths; a zero sum of products means perpendicular; proportional ratios mean parallel.
visual.caption: Only the directions matter for angles.

slides.narration: Use the cosine formula. Remember to take the modulus of the sum of products.

slides.heading: Vector equation of a line
slides.body_md: Through the point with position vector $\vec{a}$, parallel to $\vec{b}$: $\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda\vec{b}$.

visual.alt: A sketch of the axes with a fixed point A of position vector a, and a general point P on the line through A. The step from A to P is lambda times the direction vector b, and the position vector of P is r.
visual.caption: $\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda\vec{b}$ (sketch, not to scale).

slides.narration: Start at a fixed point A and move any multiple of the direction vector b. Every point you can reach this way lies on the line, and every point of the line can be reached. So the position vector r of a general point is a plus lambda times b, where lambda is any real number.

slides.heading: From vector form to Cartesian form
slides.body_md: Compare components and solve each for $\lambda$.

nodes.label: $x = x_1 + \lambda a$, $y = y_1 + \lambda b$, $z = z_1 + \lambda c$

visual.alt: Flow from the vector equation r equals a plus lambda b, to the three coordinate equations, to the Cartesian form with three equal fractions.
visual.caption: Vector form to Cartesian form in two steps.

slides.narration: Write the vector equation in components: x equals x one plus lambda a, and similarly for y and z. Solve each for lambda and set the results equal. The result is the Cartesian form, three equal fractions with the point in the numerators and the direction ratios in the denominators.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: the line through two points
slides.body_md: Write the vector and Cartesian equations of the line through $(2, -1, 4)$ and $(5, 1, 0)$.

visual.alt: Worked example 4 table: the line through 2, minus 1, 4 and 5, 1, 0 in vector form and in Cartesian form, with the point 8, 3, minus 4 obtained by putting lambda equal to 2.
visual.caption: Direction from the difference of the two points.

slides.narration: The direction is the difference of the two points, three, two and minus four. Use the first point as the fixed point. Write the vector equation, then the Cartesian equation. As a check, put lambda equal to one: you land exactly on the second point.

slides.heading: Worked example 5 of Part 1: standard form first
slides.body_md: Read the direction ratios of $\dfrac{3 - x}{4} = \dfrac{2y + 1}{6} = \dfrac{z + 2}{-3}$.

visual.alt: Table converting each fraction to standard form: 3 minus x over 4 becomes x minus 3 over minus 4; 2 y plus 1 over 6 becomes y plus one half over 3; z plus 2 over minus 3 is already standard.
visual.caption: Make each coefficient of $x$, $y$, $z$ equal to $1$ before reading.

slides.narration: Before reading a Cartesian line, make the coefficients of x, y and z equal to plus one. Three minus x over four becomes x minus three over minus four. Two y plus one over six becomes y plus one half over three. Only now can you read the direction ratios: minus four, three and minus three.

slides.heading: Quick check: vector equation of a lift cable
slides.body_md: Choose the vector equation of the cable.

visual.alt: A sketch of the axes with a fixed point A of position vector a, and a general point P on the line through A. The step from A to P is lambda times the direction vector b, and the position vector of P is r.
visual.caption: $\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda\vec{b}$ (sketch, not to scale).

slides.narration: Which vector is the fixed point, and which is the direction?

slides.heading: Quick check: name the vector
slides.body_md: Fill in the name of the vector b.

nodes.label: $x = x_1 + \lambda a$, $y = y_1 + \lambda b$, $z = z_1 + \lambda c$

visual.alt: Flow from the vector equation r equals a plus lambda b, to the three coordinate equations, to the Cartesian form with three equal fractions.
visual.caption: Vector form to Cartesian form in two steps.

slides.narration: Every point of the line is reached from a by moving a multiple of b.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: direction cosines have squares adding to 1; a line through two points has ratios equal to coordinate differences; an axis needs two equations; the angle formula; the vector and Cartesian forms.
visual.caption: Part 1 on one card.

slides.narration: To sum up. Direction cosines have squares adding to one, and ratios are any proportional set. A line through two points takes its ratios from the coordinate differences. An axis needs two equations. The angle between lines comes from the cosine formula. And a line can be written as a plus lambda b, or as three equal fractions.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Show ratios and length before cosines

nodes.label: Write ratios before cosines; show the length
Use the modulus for the acute angle
Standard form before reading a Cartesian line

visual.alt: Exam-tip flow: write the direction ratios and the length before the cosines; take the modulus for the acute angle; put a Cartesian line in standard form before reading it; check any point by substitution.
visual.caption: Most lost marks come from skipped steps.

slides.narration: In the examination, write the ratios and the length before the cosines. Use the modulus when the acute angle is asked. Always rewrite a Cartesian equation in standard form before reading it. And when you find a point, substitute it back: a quick check often saves the final mark.

decks.title: Three-Dimensional Geometry: Lines — Part 2: Intersection, distance from a line and shortest distance
goals: Decide whether two lines intersect, are parallel or are skew
Find the point of intersection of two lines
Find the foot of the perpendicular and the distance of a point from a line
Find the shortest distance between skew lines and between parallel lines

slides.heading: Three-Dimensional Geometry: Lines, Part 2
slides.body_md: When do two lines in space meet, and how far apart are they when they do not?

nodes.label: Foot and distance from a line

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: deciding whether lines are coplanar or skew, finding a point of intersection, the foot of the perpendicular and the distance of a point from a line, and the shortest distance between two lines.
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance.

slides.narration: In a plane, two lines either meet or are parallel. In space there is a third possibility: lines that are not parallel and never meet. In this part we classify pairs of lines, find where they meet, find how far a point is from a line, and measure the shortest distance between two lines.

slides.heading: What you will learn
bullets: **Foot** of the perpendicular and **distance** from a line

rows: decide whether two lines intersect, are parallel or are skew
find the point where two lines meet
find the foot of the perpendicular and the distance of a point from a line
find the shortest distance between skew or parallel lines

visual.alt: Table of the four goals of Part 2: classifying a pair of lines, finding where two lines meet, finding the foot of the perpendicular from a point, and finding shortest distances.
visual.caption: Four skills for Part 2.

slides.narration: Here are the four skills for Part 2. All of them use the same ideas from Part 1: a general point of a line, direction vectors, and the dot and cross products.

slides.heading: Skew lines
slides.body_md: Skew lines are not parallel and do not meet; they do not lie in one plane.

visual.alt: Two skew lines: L1 runs parallel to the x axis at floor level and L2 runs parallel to the y axis at height 3, above it. They never meet and are not parallel. A dashed segment MN, perpendicular to both, joins them; its length is the shortest distance.
visual.caption: Skew lines and their common perpendicular $MN$ (sketch, not to scale).

slides.narration: Picture a rail running along the floor and an overhead track crossing above it at right angles. They are not parallel, yet they never meet. Such lines are called skew lines. They do not lie in one plane. The segment that joins them at right angles to both is the shortest path between them.

slides.heading: Intersect, parallel or skew?
slides.body_md: Use $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2$ and the scalar triple product $(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \cdot (\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2)$.

nodes.label: Yes: parallel lines (or the same line)

visual.alt: Decision flow for two lines: if the direction vectors are parallel, the lines are parallel or the same; otherwise compute the scalar triple product of the difference of points with the two directions; zero means coplanar and intersecting, non-zero means skew.
visual.caption: Intersect, parallel or skew?

slides.narration: First compare the directions. If they are parallel, the lines are parallel or the same line. If not, compute the scalar triple product of the difference of the two points with the two directions. If it is zero, the lines lie in one plane, so they intersect. If it is not zero, they are skew.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: where two lines meet
slides.body_md: Show that $\vec{r} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{k} + \lambda(2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k})$ and $\vec{r} = 4\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 2\hat{k} + \mu(\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + \hat{k})$ meet, and find the point.

visual.alt: Worked example 5 table: general points of the two lines; equating x and y gives lambda equal to 1 and mu equal to minus 1; both z coordinates are then 1, so the lines meet at 3, 1, 1.
visual.caption: Two equations fix the parameters; the third decides.

slides.narration: Write a general point of each line. Equate the x coordinates and the y coordinates, and solve the two equations: lambda is one and mu is minus one. Now the decisive step: check the z coordinates. Both are one, so the lines really meet, at three, one, one. If the third equation had failed, the lines would be skew.

slides.heading: Quick check: the coplanarity test
slides.body_md: Which condition shows two non-parallel lines lie in one plane?

nodes.label: Yes: parallel lines (or the same line)

visual.alt: Decision flow for two lines: if the direction vectors are parallel, the lines are parallel or the same; otherwise compute the scalar triple product of the difference of points with the two directions; zero means coplanar and intersecting, non-zero means skew.
visual.caption: Intersect, parallel or skew?

slides.narration: Look at the second branch of the decision flow.

slides.heading: Distance of a point from a line
slides.body_md: Foot $F$: the point of the line with $\vec{PF} \perp \vec{b}$. Distance $= PF$.

visual.alt: A sketch of a straight line in space with a point P above it. A dashed segment from P meets the line at F at right angles; F is the foot of the perpendicular and PF is the distance of P from the line.
visual.caption: Foot of the perpendicular $F$ and distance $PF$ (sketch, not to scale).

slides.narration: To find how far a point P is from a line, drop a perpendicular from P to the line. It meets the line at F, called the foot of the perpendicular. Write F as a general point of the line, form the vector from P to F, and make its dot product with the direction zero. That gives lambda, the foot, and the distance.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: foot and distance
slides.body_md: Find the foot of the perpendicular from $P(7, -3, -5)$ to $\vec{r} = 2\hat{j} - \hat{k} + \lambda(\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k})$, and the distance.

visual.alt: Worked example 6 table: a general point of the line, the vector from P to it, the perpendicular condition 9 lambda minus 9 equals 0, so lambda is 1 and the foot is 1, 0, 1, and the distance is 9.
visual.caption: Make $\vec{PF}$ perpendicular to the direction.

slides.narration: A general point of the line is lambda, two minus two lambda, minus one plus two lambda. The vector from P to it must be perpendicular to the direction one, minus two, two. That gives nine lambda minus nine equals zero, so lambda is one and the foot is one, zero, one. The distance from P to the foot is nine.

slides.heading: Quick check: a sensor beside a conveyor
slides.body_md: Find the distance of the sensor from the conveyor.

visual.alt: A sketch of a straight line in space with a point P above it. A dashed segment from P meets the line at F at right angles; F is the foot of the perpendicular and PF is the distance of P from the line.
visual.caption: Foot of the perpendicular $F$ and distance $PF$ (sketch, not to scale).

slides.narration: Find lambda for the foot first, then the length of the perpendicular.

slides.heading: Shortest distance between two lines
slides.body_md: The common perpendicular gives the shortest distance.

visual.alt: Table of shortest distance formulas: for skew lines, the absolute value of the dot product of b1 cross b2 with a2 minus a1, divided by the length of b1 cross b2; for parallel lines, the length of b cross a2 minus a1 divided by the length of b; for intersecting lines the distance is zero.
visual.caption: The skew formula fails for parallel lines because $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = \vec{0}$.

slides.narration: For skew lines, the common perpendicular has the direction b one cross b two. The shortest distance is the projection of the vector joining any two points of the lines onto that direction. For parallel lines this cross product is zero, so we use a second formula with the common direction b. Intersecting lines have shortest distance zero.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: skew lines
slides.body_md: Find the shortest distance between $\vec{r} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + \lambda(2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k})$ and $\vec{r} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 3\hat{k} + \mu(2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k})$.

visual.alt: Worked example 7 table: the cross product of the directions is minus 3 i plus 6 j plus 6 k, of length 9; the difference of the points is i plus 3 k; their dot product is 15; the shortest distance is 15 over 9, which is five thirds.
visual.caption: Cross, dot, divide.

slides.narration: Cross the two directions to get minus three, six, six, whose length is nine. The vector joining the two given points is one, zero, three. Its dot product with the cross product is minus three plus eighteen, which is fifteen. Divide by nine: the shortest distance is five thirds.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: parallel lines
slides.body_md: Find the distance between $\vec{r} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k} + \lambda(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 2\hat{k})$ and $\vec{r} = 3\hat{i} + 2\hat{k} + \mu(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 2\hat{k})$.

visual.alt: Worked example 8 table: the difference of the points is 2 i minus 2 j plus 3 k; its cross product with the common direction is 2 i minus 7 j minus 6 k, of length root 89; dividing by the length 3 of the direction gives root 89 over 3.
visual.caption: Parallel lines need their own formula.

slides.narration: These lines share the direction one, two, minus two, so the skew formula cannot be used. Cross the common direction with the vector joining the two points to get two, minus seven, minus six, of length root eighty nine. Divide by the length three of the direction: the distance is root eighty nine over three.

slides.heading: Quick check: two sight-lines from one point
slides.body_md: Find the shortest distance between the two sight-lines.

visual.alt: Table of shortest distance formulas: for skew lines, the absolute value of the dot product of b1 cross b2 with a2 minus a1, divided by the length of b1 cross b2; for parallel lines, the length of b cross a2 minus a1 divided by the length of b; for intersecting lines the distance is zero.
visual.caption: The skew formula fails for parallel lines because $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = \vec{0}$.

slides.narration: Look carefully at the fixed points of the two lines before using any formula.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false
slides.body_md: Must two non-parallel lines in space meet?

visual.alt: Two skew lines: L1 runs parallel to the x axis at floor level and L2 runs parallel to the y axis at height 3, above it. They never meet and are not parallel. A dashed segment MN, perpendicular to both, joins them; its length is the shortest distance.
visual.caption: Skew lines and their common perpendicular $MN$ (sketch, not to scale).

slides.narration: Think of the floor rail and the overhead track.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2
bullets: Classify with $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2$ and the triple product
Intersection: two equations, then check the third
Skew distance: cross, dot, divide; parallel lines: their own formula

nodes.label: Intersect: solve two equations, check the third

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 2: classify the pair of lines; for intersecting lines solve two coordinate equations and check the third; for the foot make P F perpendicular to the direction; for the shortest distance cross the directions, take the dot product and divide.
visual.caption: Part 2 in one line.

slides.narration: To sum up. Classify a pair of lines using the cross product of their directions and the scalar triple product. To find where lines meet, solve two coordinate equations and check the third. For the foot of a perpendicular, make the joining vector perpendicular to the direction. For skew lines, cross, dot and divide; parallel lines need their own formula.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: State "not parallel" before calling lines skew
Show the cross product and its length
Units: give the distance in the units of the question

rows: general points 1, parameters 1, third equation checked and point 1
cross product and length 1, dot product 1, answer 1
not parallel 1, non-zero triple product or distance 1

visual.alt: Exam tips table: showing lines intersect earns marks for general points, parameters and the checked third equation; foot and distance earn marks for P F, lambda and the distance; the shortest distance earns marks for the cross product, the dot product and the answer; a skew proof needs not parallel and a non-zero distance.
visual.caption: ISC marking follows the steps.

slides.narration: In the examination, never skip the check of the third equation, because that is where intersecting and skew lines are told apart. Before calling lines skew, say that they are not parallel. Show the cross product and its length, since each earns a mark. And give the final distance in the units of the question.

notes.title: Three-Dimensional Geometry: Lines — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Direction cosines and direction ratios
sections.body_md:
- If a line makes angles $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ with the axes, its direction cosines are $l = \cos\alpha$, $m = \cos\beta$, $n = \cos\gamma$, and $l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$.
- Direction ratios $a, b, c$ are any numbers proportional to $l, m, n$: $l = \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}}$, and so on.
- Through $P(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ and $Q(x_2, y_2, z_2)$: ratios $x_2 - x_1$, $y_2 - y_1$, $z_2 - z_1$; divide by $PQ$ for the cosines.

key_terms.definition_md: Cosines of the angles a line makes with the three axes.
Any three numbers proportional to the direction cosines.

visual.alt: A three dimensional sketch with x, y and z axes drawn from the origin O, and a segment from O to a point P in space. The segment makes angles alpha, beta and gamma with the three axes.
visual.caption: $OP$ makes angles $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ with the axes: $l = \cos\alpha$, $m = \cos\beta$, $n = \cos\gamma$ (sketch, not to scale).

visuals.alt: Table: direction ratios 6, minus 3, 2 have length 7 and direction cosines 6 over 7, minus 3 over 7, 2 over 7; doubling the ratios gives length 14 and the same cosines; reversing every sign reverses the cosines.
visuals.caption: Many sets of ratios describe one line; dividing by the length gives the cosines.

visuals.alt: Worked example 1 table: the ratios are 2, 6 and minus 3; the length is 7; the direction cosines are 2 over 7, 6 over 7 and minus 3 over 7; their squares add up to 1.
visuals.caption: Subtract, measure, divide, check.

sections.heading: 2. Coordinate axes and coordinate planes
sections.body_md:
- $x$-axis: $y = 0$, $z = 0$; $y$-axis: $x = 0$, $z = 0$; $z$-axis: $x = 0$, $y = 0$.
- Vector forms: $\vec{r} = \lambda\hat{i}$, $\vec{r} = \lambda\hat{j}$, $\vec{r} = \lambda\hat{k}$.
- Coordinate planes: $xy$-plane $z = 0$; $yz$-plane $x = 0$; $zx$-plane $y = 0$.
- An axis needs **two** equations; a coordinate plane needs **one**.

key_terms.definition_md: A plane containing two of the axes, such as $z = 0$.

visual.alt: Table: the x axis is y equals 0 and z equals 0 with direction cosines 1, 0, 0; the y axis is x equals 0 and z equals 0; the z axis is x equals 0 and y equals 0; the coordinate planes are z equals 0, x equals 0 and y equals 0.
visual.caption: An axis needs two equations; a coordinate plane needs one.

visuals.alt: A sketch of the three coordinate axes from the origin. A point on the z axis is labelled 0, 0, t, showing that x and y are both zero on that axis.
visuals.caption: On the $z$-axis, $x = 0$ and $y = 0$ (sketch, not to scale).

sections.heading: 3. Angle between two lines
sections.body_md:
For direction ratios $a_1, b_1, c_1$ and $a_2, b_2, c_2$:

$\cos\theta = \dfrac{|a_1a_2 + b_1b_2 + c_1c_2|}{\sqrt{a_1^2 + b_1^2 + c_1^2}\,\sqrt{a_2^2 + b_2^2 + c_2^2}}$ (acute angle).

- **Perpendicular:** $a_1a_2 + b_1b_2 + c_1c_2 = 0$.
- **Parallel:** $\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{b_1}{b_2} = \dfrac{c_1}{c_2}$.
- A direction perpendicular to two lines: $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2$.

key_terms.definition_md: Lines whose direction ratios have zero sum of products.

headers: Condition on ratios $a_1, b_1, c_1$ and $a_2, b_2, c_2$

visual.alt: Table: the cosine of the angle between two lines is the absolute value of the sum of products of their direction ratios divided by the product of their lengths; a zero sum of products means perpendicular; proportional ratios mean parallel.
visual.caption: Only the directions matter for angles.

visuals.alt: Worked example 2 table: for ratios 1, 2, 2 and 4, 0, 3 the sum of products is 10, the lengths are 3 and 5, and the cosine of the angle is two thirds.
visuals.caption: $\theta = \cos^{-1}\dfrac23$.

visuals.alt: Worked example 3 table: ratios 2, minus 1, k and 3, 2, minus 1 are perpendicular when 6 minus 2 minus k equals 0, that is k equals 4; ratios 2, minus 1, 3 and minus 4, 2, minus 6 are parallel because each pair has ratio minus 2.
visuals.caption: Zero sum of products, or equal ratios.

sections.heading: 4. Equations of a line
sections.body_md:
- Through $\vec{a}$, parallel to $\vec{b}$: $\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda\vec{b}$; Cartesian $\dfrac{x - x_1}{a} = \dfrac{y - y_1}{b} = \dfrac{z - z_1}{c}$.
- Through two points $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$: $\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda(\vec{b} - \vec{a})$; Cartesian $\dfrac{x - x_1}{x_2 - x_1} = \dfrac{y - y_1}{y_2 - y_1} = \dfrac{z - z_1}{z_2 - z_1}$.
- **Standard form:** make the coefficients of $x$, $y$, $z$ equal to $1$ before reading the point and the ratios.
- A general point of the line is $(x_1 + a\lambda,\ y_1 + b\lambda,\ z_1 + c\lambda)$.

visual.alt: A sketch of the axes with a fixed point A of position vector a, and a general point P on the line through A. The step from A to P is lambda times the direction vector b, and the position vector of P is r.
visual.caption: $\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda\vec{b}$ (sketch, not to scale).

nodes.label: $x = x_1 + \lambda a$, $y = y_1 + \lambda b$, $z = z_1 + \lambda c$

visuals.alt: Flow from the vector equation r equals a plus lambda b, to the three coordinate equations, to the Cartesian form with three equal fractions.
visuals.caption: Vector form to Cartesian form in two steps.

visuals.alt: Worked example 4 table: the line through 2, minus 1, 4 and 5, 1, 0 in vector form and in Cartesian form, with the point 8, 3, minus 4 obtained by putting lambda equal to 2.
visuals.caption: Direction from the difference of the two points.

visuals.alt: Table converting each fraction to standard form: 3 minus x over 4 becomes x minus 3 over minus 4; 2 y plus 1 over 6 becomes y plus one half over 3; z plus 2 over minus 3 is already standard.
visuals.caption: Make each coefficient of $x$, $y$, $z$ equal to $1$ before reading.

sections.heading: 5. Coplanar and skew lines; intersection; distance from a line
sections.body_md:
- Lines $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_1 + \lambda\vec{b}_1$ and $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_2 + \mu\vec{b}_2$ with non-parallel directions are **coplanar** (and intersect) iff $(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \cdot (\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2) = 0$; otherwise they are **skew**.
- **Point of intersection:** equate general points, solve two equations for $\lambda$ and $\mu$, check the third.
- **Foot of the perpendicular** from $P$: take $F$ on the line with $\vec{PF} \cdot \vec{b} = 0$; distance $= PF$, or $\dfrac{|(\vec{P} - \vec{a}) \times \vec{b}|}{|\vec{b}|}$.
- **Image** of $P$ in the line: $2F - P$.

key_terms.definition_md: Lines that are not parallel and do not meet.
The point of the line nearest to the given point.

nodes.label: Yes: parallel lines (or the same line)

visual.alt: Decision flow for two lines: if the direction vectors are parallel, the lines are parallel or the same; otherwise compute the scalar triple product of the difference of points with the two directions; zero means coplanar and intersecting, non-zero means skew.
visual.caption: Intersect, parallel or skew?

visuals.alt: Worked example 5 table: general points of the two lines; equating x and y gives lambda equal to 1 and mu equal to minus 1; both z coordinates are then 1, so the lines meet at 3, 1, 1.
visuals.caption: Two equations fix the parameters; the third decides.

visuals.alt: A sketch of a straight line in space with a point P above it. A dashed segment from P meets the line at F at right angles; F is the foot of the perpendicular and PF is the distance of P from the line.
visuals.caption: Foot of the perpendicular $F$ and distance $PF$ (sketch, not to scale).

visuals.alt: Worked example 6 table: a general point of the line, the vector from P to it, the perpendicular condition 9 lambda minus 9 equals 0, so lambda is 1 and the foot is 1, 0, 1, and the distance is 9.
visuals.caption: Make $\vec{PF}$ perpendicular to the direction.

sections.heading: 6. Shortest distance
sections.body_md:
- **Skew lines:** $d = \dfrac{|(\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2) \cdot (\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1)|}{|\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2|}$.
- **Parallel lines** $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_1 + \lambda\vec{b}$, $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_2 + \mu\vec{b}$: $d = \dfrac{|\vec{b} \times (\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1)|}{|\vec{b}|}$.
- $d = 0$ for intersecting lines. For Cartesian lines, first read $\vec{a}_1$, $\vec{b}_1$, $\vec{a}_2$, $\vec{b}_2$.

key_terms.definition_md: The length of the common perpendicular of two lines.

visual.alt: Table of shortest distance formulas: for skew lines, the absolute value of the dot product of b1 cross b2 with a2 minus a1, divided by the length of b1 cross b2; for parallel lines, the length of b cross a2 minus a1 divided by the length of b; for intersecting lines the distance is zero.
visual.caption: The skew formula fails for parallel lines because $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = \vec{0}$.

visuals.alt: Two skew lines: L1 runs parallel to the x axis at floor level and L2 runs parallel to the y axis at height 3, above it. They never meet and are not parallel. A dashed segment MN, perpendicular to both, joins them; its length is the shortest distance.
visuals.caption: Skew lines and their common perpendicular $MN$ (sketch, not to scale).

visuals.alt: Worked example 7 table: the cross product of the directions is minus 3 i plus 6 j plus 6 k, of length 9; the difference of the points is i plus 3 k; their dot product is 15; the shortest distance is 15 over 9, which is five thirds.
visuals.caption: Cross, dot, divide.

visuals.alt: Worked example 8 table: the difference of the points is 2 i minus 2 j plus 3 k; its cross product with the common direction is 2 i minus 7 j minus 6 k, of length root 89; dividing by the length 3 of the direction gives root 89 over 3.
visuals.caption: Parallel lines need their own formula.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How ISC marks are awarded**
- *Direction cosines (2 marks):* ratios and length, then cosines.
- *Angle between lines (2 marks):* sum of products and lengths, then the angle.
- *Lines intersect (3 marks):* general points, parameters, third equation checked and the point.
- *Foot and distance (3 marks):* $\vec{PF}$, $\lambda$ and foot, distance.
- *Shortest distance (3 marks):* cross product and length, dot product, answer.

**Common mistakes**
- Reading ratios from a Cartesian line that is not in standard form.
- Forgetting the modulus for the acute angle.
- Calling lines skew without first showing they are not parallel.
- Using the skew formula for parallel lines (its denominator is $0$).
- Not checking the third equation when finding a point of intersection.

questions.stem_md: A survey drone climbs straight from a launch pad at $A(1, -2, 3)$ to a hovering point $B(5, 2, 1)$ (coordinates in metres). The direction cosines of its flight path $AB$ are
questions.solution_md: $\vec{AB} = 4\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$ and $AB = \sqrt{16 + 16 + 4} = 6$; dividing gives $\dfrac46, \dfrac46, -\dfrac26$. Option (b) gives direction ratios, not cosines.

questions.stem_md: A flagpole stands exactly along the $z$-axis of a school's coordinate model. Which pair of equations describes the line of the flagpole?
questions.solution_md: Every point of the $z$-axis has the form $(0, 0, t)$: both $x$ and $y$ are zero. A single equation $z = 0$ is a plane, and $x = 0$, $z = 0$ is the $y$-axis.

questions.stem_md: In a model of a hall, the floor is the $xy$-plane and one wall contains the $x$- and $z$-axes. Which equation describes the plane of that wall?
questions.solution_md: Points on the $x$-axis $(t, 0, 0)$ and the $z$-axis $(0, 0, s)$ all have $y = 0$, so the wall is the plane $y = 0$ (the $xz$-plane).

questions.stem_md: A spotlight beam in a museum makes equal acute angles with the three coordinate axes. Its direction cosines are
questions.solution_md: Equal angles give $l = m = n$ and $3l^2 = 1$, so $l = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$ (positive for acute angles). The other triples do not have squares adding up to $1$.

questions.stem_md: A ropeway cable has direction cosines $l = \dfrac27$, $m = -\dfrac37$ and an unknown $n$. What are the possible values of $n$?
questions.solution_md: $n^2 = 1 - \dfrac{4}{49} - \dfrac{9}{49} = \dfrac{36}{49}$, so $n = \pm\dfrac67$. Both signs give a valid direction; the sign depends on which way the cable is described.

questions.stem_md: Three markers on a straight metro tunnel bore are at $P(3, 0, -2)$, $Q(6, 6, 0)$ and $R(9, 12, 2)$. What do the direction ratios of $PQ$ and $QR$ tell the engineer?

options.text_md: They are equal, so $P$, $Q$, $R$ are collinear
They are perpendicular, so the bore turns through a right angle at $Q$
They are not proportional, so the bore bends at $Q$

questions.solution_md: $PQ$: $3, 6, 2$ and $QR$: $3, 6, 2$. Equal (hence proportional) ratios through the common point $Q$ mean one straight line.

questions.stem_md: Two laser beams at a science fair have direction ratios $2, 2, 1$ and $2, -1, -2$. The angle between the beams is
questions.solution_md: $a_1a_2 + b_1b_2 + c_1c_2 = 4 - 2 - 2 = 0$, so $\cos\theta = 0$ and the beams are perpendicular.

questions.stem_md: A roof truss has one strut along direction ratios $1, 1, 0$ and another along $0, 1, 1$. The acute angle between the struts is
questions.solution_md: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{|0 + 1 + 0|}{\sqrt2\,\sqrt2} = \dfrac12$, so $\theta = 60^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: For which value of $k$ is the line $\dfrac{x - 2}{3} = \dfrac{y + 1}{k} = \dfrac{z}{2}$ perpendicular to the line $\dfrac{x}{1} = \dfrac{y - 4}{2} = \dfrac{z + 3}{-5}$?
questions.solution_md: $3(1) + k(2) + 2(-5) = 0 \Rightarrow 2k = 7 \Rightarrow k = \dfrac72$.

questions.stem_md: Two straight conveyor belts in a warehouse run along direction ratios $3, -6, 9$ and $-1, p, -3$. If the belts are parallel, $p$ equals
questions.solution_md: Parallel lines have proportional ratios: $\dfrac{-1}{3} = \dfrac{p}{-6} = \dfrac{-3}{9}$, so $p = 2$.

questions.stem_md: A hiking trail map shows a footbridge from $A(0, 1, 2)$ to $B(2, 3, 3)$ and a zipline from $C(1, 0, 0)$ to $D(5, 3, 0)$. The cosine of the acute angle between the footbridge and the zipline is
questions.solution_md: Ratios $2, 2, 1$ (length $3$) and $4, 3, 0$ (length $5$): $\cos\theta = \dfrac{8 + 6 + 0}{3 \times 5} = \dfrac{14}{15}$.

questions.stem_md: A lift cable passes through the point $(3, -1, 2)$ and runs parallel to $2\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} - \hat{k}$. Its vector equation is
questions.solution_md: $\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda\vec{b}$ with $\vec{a}$ the position vector of the given point and $\vec{b}$ the given direction. Option (a) swaps their roles.

questions.stem_md: A straight drainage pipe is laid from $(4, 0, -3)$ to $(1, 2, 5)$. Its Cartesian equations are
questions.solution_md: Direction ratios are the differences $1 - 4 = -3$, $2 - 0 = 2$, $5 - (-3) = 8$; use either point in the numerators. Option (d) loses the sign of $-3$.

questions.stem_md: A rescue team plots a straight search line $\dfrac{x + 2}{3} = \dfrac{y - 1}{-2} = \dfrac{z - 4}{5}$. Which of these points lies on it?
questions.solution_md: For $(4, -3, 14)$: $\dfrac63 = \dfrac{-4}{-2} = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2$, the same value in each fraction. For $(1, -1, 10)$ the fractions are $1, 1, \dfrac65$.

questions.stem_md: A cable run is given as $\dfrac{3 - x}{4} = \dfrac{2y + 1}{6} = \dfrac{z + 2}{-3}$. After writing it in standard form, its direction ratios are
questions.solution_md: Make each coefficient $1$: $\dfrac{x - 3}{-4} = \dfrac{y + \frac12}{3} = \dfrac{z + 2}{-3}$. So the ratios are $-4, 3, -3$. Option (d) reads the denominators without this step.

questions.stem_md: A tunnel-boring machine moves along $\vec{r} = \hat{i} - 3\hat{k} + \lambda(2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 4\hat{k})$. The same path in Cartesian form is
questions.solution_md: The point is $(1, 0, -3)$ and the direction ratios are $2, -1, 4$; write $\dfrac{x - x_1}{a} = \dfrac{y - y_1}{b} = \dfrac{z - z_1}{c}$.

questions.stem_md: Two straight steel cables in a stadium roof are not parallel and never meet. Such a pair of lines is called
questions.solution_md: Lines in space that are neither parallel nor intersecting do not lie in one plane; they are skew lines.

questions.stem_md: The flight paths $\vec{r} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k} + \lambda(\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k})$ and $\vec{r} = 4\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 7\hat{k} + \mu(\hat{i} + \hat{j})$ of two model aircraft cross each other. At which point?
questions.solution_md: Equate components: $1 + \lambda = 4 + \mu$, $2 - \lambda = 1 + \mu$, $3 + 2\lambda = 7$. The third gives $\lambda = 2$, the second $\mu = -1$, and the first checks: $3 = 3$. The point is $(3, 0, 7)$.

questions.stem_md: Lines $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_1 + \lambda\vec{b}_1$ and $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_2 + \mu\vec{b}_2$ have non-parallel directions. Which condition tells a designer that the two lines lie in one plane, so that they meet?
questions.solution_md: The lines are coplanar when $\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1$, $\vec{b}_1$ and $\vec{b}_2$ lie in one plane, i.e. their scalar triple product is $0$. Option (d) is perpendicularity and (a) is parallelism.

questions.stem_md: A lamp at $P(4, 4, 7)$ hangs near a straight rail $\dfrac{x - 1}{1} = \dfrac{y}{2} = \dfrac{z + 1}{2}$. The foot of the perpendicular from the lamp to the rail is
questions.solution_md: A general rail point is $(1 + \lambda, 2\lambda, -1 + 2\lambda)$. The joining vector $(\lambda - 3, 2\lambda - 4, 2\lambda - 8)$ is perpendicular to $(1, 2, 2)$: $9\lambda - 27 = 0$, so $\lambda = 3$ and the foot is $(4, 6, 5)$.

questions.stem_md: In a warehouse, a ground rail runs along $\vec{r} = \hat{i} + \lambda\hat{j}$ and an overhead crane track along $\vec{r} = 5\hat{k} + \mu\hat{i}$ (metres). The shortest distance between them is
questions.solution_md: $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = \hat{j} \times \hat{i} = -\hat{k}$, $\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1 = -\hat{i} + 5\hat{k}$; $d = \dfrac{|(-\hat{i} + 5\hat{k}) \cdot (-\hat{k})|}{1} = 5$.

questions.stem_md: Two parallel guide wires of a ski lift follow $\vec{r} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \lambda(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k})$ and $\vec{r} = 3\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k} + \mu(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k})$. The distance between the wires is
questions.solution_md: $\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1 = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$; $\vec{b} \times (\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) = -2\hat{i} + 6\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}$ of length $\sqrt{65}$; divide by $|\vec{b}| = 3$. Option (c) forgets to divide.

questions.stem_md: An engineer compares the formula sheets of two students for the shortest distance between non-parallel lines $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_1 + \lambda\vec{b}_1$ and $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_2 + \mu\vec{b}_2$. Which formula is correct?
questions.solution_md: The shortest distance is the projection of $\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1$ on the common perpendicular, whose direction is $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2$. Option (a) is only the distance between the two chosen points.

questions.stem_md: Two survey sight-lines both start from the same theodolite point: $\vec{r} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \lambda(\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k})$ and $\vec{r} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \mu(3\hat{i} + \hat{k})$. The shortest distance between these lines is
questions.solution_md: Both lines pass through $(2, 1, 0)$, so they intersect there and the shortest distance is $0$ (also $\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1 = \vec{0}$ in the formula).

questions.stem_md: A support beam must be perpendicular to two girders with direction ratios $1, 2, 3$ and $3, 2, 1$. Suitable direction ratios for the beam are
questions.solution_md: $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = (2 - 6)\hat{i} - (1 - 9)\hat{j} + (2 - 6)\hat{k} = -4\hat{i} + 8\hat{j} - 4\hat{k}$, proportional to $1, -2, 1$. Check: $1 - 4 + 3 = 0$ and $3 - 4 + 1 = 0$.

questions.stem_md: A skylight frame edge satisfies $x = 2y = 3z$. Its direction ratios are
questions.solution_md: Put $x = 2y = 3z = t$: the points are $\left(t, \dfrac t2, \dfrac t3\right)$, so the ratios are $1 : \dfrac12 : \dfrac13 = 6 : 3 : 2$. Option (c) uses the coefficients themselves.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A line with direction ratios $2, -1, 2$ has direction cosines $\dfrac23, -\dfrac13, \dfrac23$.

**Reason (R):** Direction cosines are found by dividing the direction ratios by $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}$.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: $\sqrt{4 + 1 + 4} = 3$, and dividing $2, -1, 2$ by $3$ gives the cosines in A; R is exactly the rule used, so it explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Lines with direction ratios $1, 2, -3$ and $-2, -4, 5$ are parallel.

**Reason (R):** Two lines are parallel when their direction ratios are proportional.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true. A is false: $\dfrac{-2}{1} = \dfrac{-4}{2} = -2$ but $\dfrac{5}{-3} \ne -2$, so the ratios are not proportional and the lines are not parallel.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The search line $\dfrac{x - 1}{2} = \dfrac{y + 3}{-1} = \dfrac{z - 4}{3}$ passes through the point $(1, -3, 4)$.

**Reason (R):** The direction ratios of this line are $1, -3, 4$.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: Putting $(1, -3, 4)$ makes every fraction $0$, so A is true. R is false: the direction ratios are the denominators $2, -1, 3$; $(1, -3, 4)$ is a point.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The lines $\vec{r} = \hat{i} + \lambda\hat{j}$ and $\vec{r} = 5\hat{k} + \mu\hat{i}$ are skew.

**Reason (R):** The direction vectors $\hat{j}$ and $\hat{i}$ of these lines are not parallel.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: they are not parallel and their shortest distance is $5 \ne 0$, so they do not meet. R is true, but non-parallel lines may still intersect; R alone does not explain why they are skew.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The shortest distance between $\vec{r} = 3\hat{i} - \hat{k} + \lambda(2\hat{i} + \hat{j})$ and $\vec{r} = 3\hat{i} - \hat{k} + \mu(\hat{j} + 4\hat{k})$ is $0$.

**Reason (R):** Two lines through a common point intersect.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: Both lines pass through $(3, 0, -1)$, so they intersect and the shortest distance is $0$; R gives exactly this reason.

questions.stem_md: True or false: the numbers $\dfrac{3}{13}, \dfrac{4}{13}, \dfrac{12}{13}$ can be the direction cosines of a kite string.
True or false: if $a_1a_2 + b_1b_2 + c_1c_2 = 0$ for the direction ratios of two lines, the lines are parallel.
questions.solution_md: False. A zero sum of products means the lines are **perpendicular**; parallel lines have proportional direction ratios.

questions.stem_md: True or false: two lines in space that are not parallel must meet at a point.
questions.solution_md: False. In space, non-parallel lines can be skew: for example $\vec{r} = \hat{i} + \lambda\hat{j}$ and $\vec{r} = 5\hat{k} + \mu\hat{i}$ never meet.

questions.stem_md: The $y$-axis has direction cosines $0$, ____, $0$.
questions.solution_md: The $y$-axis makes angles $90^\circ$, $0^\circ$, $90^\circ$ with the axes, so its direction cosines are $0, 1, 0$.

questions.stem_md: In the equation $\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda\vec{b}$ of a line, the vector $\vec{b}$ is called the ____ vector of the line.
questions.solution_md: $\vec{b}$ is the direction (parallel) vector: every point of the line is reached from $\vec{a}$ by moving a multiple of $\vec{b}$.

questions.stem_md: A road on a flyover and a road on the ground beneath it are straight, not parallel, and never cross. As lines in space they are called ____ lines.
questions.solution_md: Such lines are called skew lines; they do not lie in one plane.

questions.stem_md: A guy wire is stretched straight from $P(1, 2, -3)$ to $Q(7, 4, 0)$ (metres). Find its length in metres.
The point $(k, 1, 7)$ lies on the straight cable $\dfrac{x - 3}{2} = \dfrac{y + 5}{3} = \dfrac{z - 1}{3}$. Find $k$.
questions.solution_md: From $y$: $\dfrac{1 + 5}{3} = 2$; from $z$: $\dfrac{7 - 1}{3} = 2$. So $\lambda = 2$ and $x = 3 + 2 \times 2 = 7$, i.e. $k = 7$.

questions.stem_md: A sensor at $P(8, 5, 0)$ monitors a straight conveyor $\vec{r} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \lambda(2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k})$. Find the perpendicular distance of the sensor from the conveyor.

Two drones fly along $\vec{r} = \hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k} + \lambda(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k})$ and $\vec{r} = \hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 2\hat{k} + \mu(2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k})$ (units in metres). Find the shortest distance between their paths.
questions.solution_md: $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = -6\hat{i} + 6\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$, $|\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2| = 9$; $\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1 = 6\hat{j}$ gives a dot product of $36$; $d = \dfrac{36}{9} = 4$ m.

questions.stem_md: For which value of $k$ is a line with direction ratios $k, 2, 3$ perpendicular to a line with direction ratios $2, -5, 4$?

questions.stem_md: A zipline runs straight from $A(-2, 4, 1)$ to $B(4, 1, 3)$. Find the direction cosines of the zipline $AB$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Direction ratios: $4 - (-2) = 6$, $1 - 4 = -3$, $3 - 1 = 2$. Length $\sqrt{36 + 9 + 4} = 7$.

Direction cosines: $\dfrac{6}{7}, -\dfrac{3}{7}, \dfrac{2}{7}$.

questions.solution_md: Differences of coordinates, then divide by the length.

questions.stem_md: Three poles of a straight fence are planned at $A(1, -2, 3)$, $B(3, 1, 2)$ and $C(7, 7, 0)$. Use direction ratios to show that the poles are in one straight line.

answer.model_answer_md:
$AB$: $2, 3, -1$. $BC$: $4, 6, -2 = 2(2, 3, -1)$.

The ratios are proportional, so $AB \parallel BC$; since they share the point $B$, the points $A$, $B$, $C$ are collinear.

questions.solution_md: Proportional ratios plus a common point.

questions.stem_md: A hang-glider's two tow lines follow $\dfrac{x}{2} = \dfrac{y}{2} = \dfrac{z}{1}$ and $\dfrac{x - 5}{4} = \dfrac{y + 2}{1} = \dfrac{z - 3}{8}$. Find the angle between the tow lines.

answer.model_answer_md:
Ratios $2, 2, 1$ (length $3$) and $4, 1, 8$ (length $9$).

$\cos\theta = \dfrac{|8 + 2 + 8|}{3 \times 9} = \dfrac{18}{27} = \dfrac23$, so $\theta = \cos^{-1}\dfrac23$.

questions.solution_md: Use the cosine formula with the direction ratios.

questions.stem_md: A new pipe must pass through the valve at $P(2, -3, 5)$ and run parallel to the existing pipe $\dfrac{x - 1}{4} = \dfrac{y + 2}{-1} = \dfrac{z}{3}$. Write the vector and Cartesian equations of the new pipe.

answer.model_answer_md:
Direction ratios $4, -1, 3$ (from the existing pipe).

Vector: $\vec{r} = 2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 5\hat{k} + \lambda(4\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 3\hat{k})$.

Cartesian: $\dfrac{x - 2}{4} = \dfrac{y + 3}{-1} = \dfrac{z - 5}{3}$.

questions.solution_md: Same direction as the given line, through the new point.

questions.stem_md: A mine shaft is drilled in a straight line from $A(-1, 3, 2)$ towards $B(2, 5, -4)$. Find the point where the shaft meets the $xy$-plane.

answer.model_answer_md:
Line: $\dfrac{x + 1}{3} = \dfrac{y - 3}{2} = \dfrac{z - 2}{-6} = \lambda$, so a general point is $(-1 + 3\lambda, 3 + 2\lambda, 2 - 6\lambda)$.

On the $xy$-plane $z = 0$: $\lambda = \dfrac13$, giving $\left(0, \dfrac{11}{3}, 0\right)$.

questions.solution_md: General point of the line, then set z = 0.

questions.stem_md: Show that the two cable runs $\vec{r} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{k} + \lambda(\hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k})$ and $\vec{r} = 3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k} + \mu(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j})$ lie in one plane.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}$, $\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1 = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j}$.

$(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \cdot (\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2) = 2 - 2 + 0 = 0$, so the lines are coplanar.

questions.solution_md: Scalar triple product equal to zero.

questions.stem_md: Two parallel rails of an imagined funicular are $\dfrac{x - 1}{2} = \dfrac{y + 1}{-1} = \dfrac{z}{2}$ and $\dfrac{x - 4}{2} = \dfrac{y - 2}{-1} = \dfrac{z + 3}{2}$. Find the distance between the rails.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$, $|\vec{b}| = 3$; $\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1 = 3\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$.

$\vec{b} \times (\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) = -3\hat{i} + 12\hat{j} + 9\hat{k}$, of length $\sqrt{234} = 3\sqrt{26}$.

$d = \dfrac{3\sqrt{26}}{3} = \sqrt{26}$.

questions.solution_md: Parallel-lines formula.

questions.stem_md: A beam joins $P(1, -1, 2)$ to $Q(3, 4, -2)$, and a strut joins $R(0, 3, 2)$ to $S(3, 5, 6)$. Show that the beam is perpendicular to the strut.
questions.solution_md: Zero sum of products of direction ratios.

questions.stem_md: A surveyor at the origin looks at a straight boundary wall $\vec{r} = \hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 2\hat{k} + \lambda(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j})$. Find the foot of the perpendicular from the origin to the wall and its distance from the origin.

answer.model_answer_md:
General point $F = (1 + \lambda, -3 + 2\lambda, 2)$. $\vec{OF} \cdot (1, 2, 0) = 0$: $(1 + \lambda) + 2(-3 + 2\lambda) = 0 \Rightarrow 5\lambda = 5 \Rightarrow \lambda = 1$.

$F = (2, -1, 2)$, distance $\sqrt{4 + 1 + 4} = 3$.

questions.solution_md: Perpendicularity condition gives λ.

questions.stem_md: A camera drone's line of sight makes $60^\circ$ with the $x$-axis and $60^\circ$ with the $y$-axis. Find the angle it makes with the $z$-axis (both possibilities) and its direction cosines in each case.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\cos^2 60^\circ + \cos^2 60^\circ + \cos^2\gamma = 1 \Rightarrow \dfrac14 + \dfrac14 + \cos^2\gamma = 1 \Rightarrow \cos^2\gamma = \dfrac12$.

$\cos\gamma = \pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$, so $\gamma = 45^\circ$ or $135^\circ$.

Direction cosines: $\dfrac12, \dfrac12, \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$ or $\dfrac12, \dfrac12, -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$.

questions.solution_md: Use l² + m² + n² = 1.

questions.stem_md: Two straight hiking trails are $\dfrac{x + 1}{2} = \dfrac{y - 3}{p} = \dfrac{z}{-1}$ and $\dfrac{x - 4}{p} = \dfrac{y + 2}{3} = \dfrac{z - 1}{4}$. Find $p$ if the trails are perpendicular, and then write integer direction ratios of the first trail.

answer.model_answer_md:
Perpendicular: $2p + 3p + (-1)(4) = 0 \Rightarrow 5p = 4 \Rightarrow p = \dfrac45$.

First trail ratios: $2, \dfrac45, -1$; multiply by $5$: $10, 4, -5$.

questions.solution_md: Sum of products equals zero; then clear the fraction.

questions.stem_md: A light rail line is recorded as $\dfrac{2x - 3}{4} = \dfrac{1 - y}{2} = \dfrac{3z + 6}{9}$. Write it in standard Cartesian form, state a point on it and its direction ratios, and write its vector equation.

answer.model_answer_md:
Divide to make each coefficient $1$: $\dfrac{x - \frac32}{2} = \dfrac{y - 1}{-2} = \dfrac{z + 2}{3}$.

Point $\left(\dfrac32, 1, -2\right)$; direction ratios $2, -2, 3$.

Vector form: $\vec{r} = \dfrac32\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k} + \lambda(2\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k})$.

questions.solution_md: Standard form first, then read point and ratios.

questions.stem_md: Two irrigation pipes follow $\dfrac{x - 2}{1} = \dfrac{y + 1}{2} = \dfrac{z - 3}{-1}$ and $\dfrac{x + 1}{2} = \dfrac{y - 3}{-1} = \dfrac{z + 4}{3}$. Show that they meet and find the junction point.

answer.model_answer_md:
General points: $(2 + \lambda, -1 + 2\lambda, 3 - \lambda)$ and $(-1 + 2\mu, 3 - \mu, -4 + 3\mu)$.

Equate $x$ and $y$: $2 + \lambda = -1 + 2\mu$ and $-1 + 2\lambda = 3 - \mu$, giving $\lambda = 1$, $\mu = 2$.

Check $z$: $3 - 1 = 2$ and $-4 + 6 = 2$ ✓. The pipes meet at $(3, 1, 2)$.

questions.solution_md: Solve two coordinate equations; verify the third.

questions.stem_md: A Wi-Fi router at $P(2, 2, 6)$ is to be wired to the nearest point of a straight cable tray $\dfrac{x + 1}{2} = \dfrac{y - 2}{-2} = \dfrac{z - 3}{1}$. Find that nearest point (the foot of the perpendicular) and the length of wire needed.

answer.model_answer_md:
General point $F = (-1 + 2\lambda, 2 - 2\lambda, 3 + \lambda)$; $\vec{PF} = (2\lambda - 3, -2\lambda, \lambda - 3)$.

$\vec{PF} \cdot (2, -2, 1) = 0$: $4\lambda - 6 + 4\lambda + \lambda - 3 = 0 \Rightarrow 9\lambda = 9 \Rightarrow \lambda = 1$.

$F = (1, 0, 4)$; length $PF = \sqrt{1 + 4 + 4} = 3$.

questions.solution_md: Perpendicular condition, then the distance.

questions.stem_md: Two straight ducts in an imagined factory ceiling are $\vec{r} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k} + \lambda(\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k})$ and $\vec{r} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} - \hat{k} + \mu(2\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 2\hat{k})$. Show that the ducts are skew.

answer.model_answer_md:
Directions $1, -1, 1$ and $2, 1, 2$ are not proportional, so the ducts are not parallel.

$\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = -3\hat{i} + 3\hat{k}$, $\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1 = \hat{i} - 3\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$; $(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \cdot (\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2) = -3 - 6 = -9 \ne 0$.

So the shortest distance $\dfrac{9}{3\sqrt2} = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt2} \ne 0$: the ducts never meet and are skew.

questions.solution_md: Not parallel, and the triple product is non-zero.

questions.stem_md: Two zipline cables at an adventure park follow $\vec{r} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{k} + \lambda(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k})$ and $\vec{r} = 3\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \mu(2\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + \hat{k})$ (metres). Find the shortest distance between the cables.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = 6\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 6\hat{k}$, $|\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2| = 9$.

$\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1 = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$; dot product $12 + 3 + 12 = 27$.

$d = \dfrac{27}{9} = 3$ m.

questions.solution_md: Skew-lines formula.

questions.stem_md: A lab technician aims two laser pointers along $\dfrac{x - 1}{1} = \dfrac{y + 2}{3} = \dfrac{z - 4}{-1}$ and $\dfrac{x - 4}{2} = \dfrac{y}{-1} = \dfrac{z - 4}{1}$. Compute the shortest distance between the beams and say what it tells you.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = (3 - 1)\hat{i} - (1 + 2)\hat{j} + (-1 - 6)\hat{k} = 2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} - 7\hat{k}$.

$\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1 = 3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j}$; dot product $6 - 6 + 0 = 0$.

So $d = 0$: the beams meet (at $(2, 1, 3)$).

questions.solution_md: Zero shortest distance with non-parallel directions means intersecting lines.

questions.stem_md: A drainage channel must start at $(2, -1, 3)$ and be perpendicular to two existing channels with direction ratios $2, 1, -1$ and $1, -1, 2$. Find its vector equation.

answer.model_answer_md:
Direction $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = (2 - 1)\hat{i} - (4 + 1)\hat{j} + (-2 - 1)\hat{k} = \hat{i} - 5\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$.

Check: $2 - 5 + 3 = 0$ and $1 + 5 - 6 = 0$.

$\vec{r} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 3\hat{k} + \lambda(\hat{i} - 5\hat{j} - 3\hat{k})$.

questions.solution_md: Cross product gives a direction perpendicular to both.

questions.stem_md: In a classroom model of a room, write (i) the Cartesian equations of the $y$-axis, (ii) the vector equation of the $x$-axis, and (iii) the equation of the $yz$-plane.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) $y$-axis: $x = 0$, $z = 0$ (equivalently $\dfrac x0 = \dfrac y1 = \dfrac z0$).

(ii) $x$-axis: $\vec{r} = \lambda\hat{i}$.

(iii) $yz$-plane: $x = 0$.

questions.solution_md: Points of each axis or plane have the stated coordinates zero.

questions.stem_md:
Two straight tunnels of an imagined hill railway are $\dfrac{x + 1}{2} = \dfrac{y - 4}{-1} = \dfrac{z + 4}{2}$ and $\dfrac{x - 5}{2} = \dfrac{y - 7}{2} = \dfrac{z + 4}{-1}$.

(a) Show that the tunnels meet and find the point where they meet. [3]

(b) Find the angle between the tunnels. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** General points: $(-1 + 2\lambda, 4 - \lambda, -4 + 2\lambda)$ and $(5 + 2\mu, 7 + 2\mu, -4 - \mu)$.

From $x$: $2\lambda - 2\mu = 6$; from $y$: $-\lambda - 2\mu = 3$. Subtracting, $3\lambda = 3$, so $\lambda = 1$, $\mu = -2$.

$z$: $-4 + 2 = -2$ and $-4 + 2 = -2$ ✓. They meet at $(1, 3, -2)$.

**(b)** $2(2) + (-1)(2) + 2(-1) = 0$, so the angle is $90^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: Solve two equations, check the third; dot product of directions.

questions.stem_md:
A security camera at $P(5, 7, 0)$ watches a straight fence $\vec{r} = -\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \lambda(2\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 2\hat{k})$.

(a) Find the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to the fence and the perpendicular distance. [3]

(b) A mirror image of the camera is to be drawn on the other side of the fence, at the reflection of $P$ in the line. Find its coordinates. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** General point $F = (-1 + 2\lambda, 1 + \lambda, 2\lambda)$; $\vec{PF} = (2\lambda - 6, \lambda - 6, 2\lambda)$.

$\vec{PF} \cdot (2, 1, 2) = 4\lambda - 12 + \lambda - 6 + 4\lambda = 9\lambda - 18 = 0 \Rightarrow \lambda = 2$.

$F = (3, 3, 4)$; $PF = \sqrt{4 + 16 + 16} = 6$.

**(b)** $F$ is the midpoint of $P$ and its image $P'$: $P' = 2F - P = (6 - 5, 6 - 7, 8 - 0) = (1, -1, 8)$.

questions.solution_md: Foot by perpendicularity; image by the midpoint formula.

questions.stem_md:
Two cable cars cross a valley along $\vec{r} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k} + \lambda(2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k})$ and $\vec{r} = 3\hat{i} - \hat{j} - \hat{k} + \mu(\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k})$ (units: tens of metres).

(a) Find the shortest distance between the two cable lines. [3]

(b) Write both lines in Cartesian form and state, with a reason, whether the cables can touch. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = (4 + 2)\hat{i} - (4 - 1)\hat{j} + (-4 - 2)\hat{k} = 6\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} - 6\hat{k}$, of length $9$.

$\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1 = \hat{i} - 2\hat{k}$; dot product $6 + 0 + 12 = 18$.

$d = \dfrac{18}{9} = 2$ units, that is $20$ m.

**(b)** $\dfrac{x - 2}{2} = \dfrac{y + 1}{2} = \dfrac{z - 1}{1}$ and $\dfrac{x - 3}{1} = \dfrac{y + 1}{-2} = \dfrac{z + 1}{2}$.

The shortest distance is not zero (and the directions are not parallel), so the lines are skew: the cables cannot touch.

questions.solution_md: Skew-lines formula; non-zero distance means no meeting point.

questions.stem_md:
Two delivery drones over an imagined town move in straight lines: drone A along $\vec{r} = 10\hat{k} + \lambda(\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k})$ and drone B along $\vec{r} = 3\hat{j} + 16\hat{k} + \mu(2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k})$ (metres).

(a) By equating coordinates, show that the paths do not cross. [2]

(b) Find the closest distance between the two paths. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $x$: $\lambda = 2\mu$; $y$: $-2\lambda = 3 + 2\mu$. Then $-4\mu = 3 + 2\mu$, so $\mu = -\dfrac12$, $\lambda = -1$.

$z$: $10 + 2\lambda = 8$ but $16 + \mu = 15.5$; these differ, so the paths do not meet.

**(b)** $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = -6\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}$, of length $9$; $\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1 = 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}$, dot product $9 + 36 = 45$.

$d = \dfrac{45}{9} = 5$ m.

questions.solution_md: Inconsistent third equation; then the skew-lines formula.

questions.stem_md:
A stage designer needs a light bar through $P(1, -1, 2)$ that is perpendicular to two existing bars with directions $\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$ and $\hat{i} - \hat{j}$.

(a) Find the vector and Cartesian equations of the light bar. [3]

(b) Will the light bar pass through the hook at $(4, 2, -4)$? Justify. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Direction $(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}) \times (\hat{i} - \hat{j}) = (0 + 1)\hat{i} - (0 - 1)\hat{j} + (-1 - 1)\hat{k} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$.

Vector: $\vec{r} = \hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k} + \lambda(\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k})$. Cartesian: $\dfrac{x - 1}{1} = \dfrac{y + 1}{1} = \dfrac{z - 2}{-2}$.

**(b)** At $(4, 2, -4)$: $\dfrac{3}{1} = \dfrac{3}{1} = \dfrac{-6}{-2} = 3$. All three fractions are equal, so the bar passes through the hook ($\lambda = 3$).
